sections.h2: Selling a house in Susquehanna Township
sections.html:
Susquehanna Township lies north of Harrisburg in Dauphin County and uses the ZIP codes 17109 and 17110. It is a first-class township. A sale here involves three offices: the township for permits, the county treasurer for tax bills, and the Dauphin County recorder for the deed.

Knowing which office holds which record saves phone tag. Each is covered below, plus the steps that tend to slow a closing and what a cash sale does and does not skip.

The township counts 28,434 residents, up 6.2 percent from the 26,762 of April 2020. Homeowners occupy 62.9 percent of the housing, and the middle owned home is valued at $227,100. Median rent is $1,487, household income is $84,832, and the 11,894 households average 2.26 people.

Close to 37 percent of homes are rented, so landlords shop alongside owner-occupants. If the house is occupied, tell each buyer up front who lives there and on what lease terms.

Residential permits go to the municipal office at 1900 Linglestown Road in Harrisburg, and the number for questions is 717-909-9251. Every application needs a site plan.

Pennsylvania enforces the 2021 International Construction Codes, so repairs you do now follow that edition. For existing houses, code enforcement uses the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, which the township adopted on July 14, 2022, effective July 19, 2022.

A contractor who disagrees with a ruling can appeal to the Joint Uniform Construction Code Appeals Board. It hears cases as needed on the fourth Tuesday of each month at 5 p.m. in the Hampden Township Municipal Building in Mechanicsburg.

The township has also been working on a Linglestown Road Overlay zoning amendment. If your house sits along that corridor, call the township about the final text before you list.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax and what transfer tax applies?
sections.html:
In this township the Dauphin County Treasurer acts as tax collector. The office is at 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg, phone 717-780-6550.

Dauphin County realty transfer tax split on a Susquehanna Township sale
RecipientShare of sale price
State (Department of Revenue)1.0%
Municipality0.5%
School district0.5%
Total2.0%

The county Recorder of Deeds can confirm that split and keeps deeds dating to 1785. It sits in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Room 102, phone 717-780-6560. Recording fees can be paid in cash or by check. Transfers between family members are generally exempt.

Before closing, find out from the treasurer exactly what your parcel owes. Whatever it is gets subtracted from your proceeds by the title company.

Susquehanna became a first-class township by Dauphin County Court order on January 2, 1952, and a nine-member Board of Commissioners elected by ward runs it today. Zoning decisions can be appealed to a Zoning Hearing Board, and a separate Township Authority also meets regularly.

Agendas and minutes for all three bodies are posted in the township's online Agenda Center. A seller facing a zoning question can read what has already been decided on similar properties before spending money on an application.

sections.h2: What to line up before closing
sections.html:
Title agents and buyers ask for the same handful of records, each from a different office. Begin gathering them the day a contract is signed.

  • A copy of your deed from the county recorder, and a payoff letter from the bank that holds your loan.
  • The current tax balance from the treasurer's office.
  • Permit records for decks, additions or finished space, from the municipal office on Linglestown Road.
  • Lease copies and tenant contact details, if anyone rents the house.

An inherited house adds one more step. Whoever holds legal authority over the estate must sign, so settle that question before a buyer fixes a closing date.

A tax debt will not stop a sale, only reduce what you walk away with. The title search turns up the balance, and settlement pays it out of the sale money. Call the treasurer early and ask for the figure in writing.

If you are well behind and the house is already headed toward a tax sale, a quick sale for cash can be the way to stay ahead of that deadline. Mention any other claims against the parcel to the closing agent, an unpaid contractor bill for example, since those get cleared at the same settlement.

Sellers who are current on taxes have an easier path: a clean balance letter means the title search finishes faster and the settlement date is less likely to move.

sections.h2: How a sale unfolds, step by step
sections.html:
1. Both sides sign an agreement of sale naming the price, the settlement date and the person who covers transfer tax.
  2. A title search combs the record for liens, mortgages and tax balances.
  3. The buyer's inspector or lender asks for permit records, so the township office gets a call from your side first.
  4. At settlement you sign over the deed, the loan and any tax debt are paid off, and the remainder is yours.
  5. The new deed is filed with the recorder at the Harrisburg courthouse.

With a cash buyer there is no bank appraisal or underwriting queue, and that queue is where many closings stall. The search, the payoff and the recording still take their normal time.

Because so many homes in the township are rented, an occupied sale is common. Start by reading the lease for its end date and its notice terms. A buyer who plans to live in the house will need the tenant out by closing, and an investor may want the lease to stay in place.

Give showing notice in writing and keep the tenant informed about timing. A cooperative tenant makes inspections and the final walk-through much smoother, and a direct buyer who takes the house as is will usually work around an existing lease instead of asking you to clear it first.

A direct sale skips open houses and lets you choose the closing day. A listing reaches the widest group of buyers. Plenty of local sellers are juggling an inherited house, a tenant or repairs they would rather not fund.

  • Pull your deed copy from the county and request a loan payoff before talking to buyers.
  • Walk the house against the 2021 maintenance code and fix peeling paint, broken steps and loose railings.
  • Write into the offer who pays the 2 percent transfer tax.
  • Put a listing's likely net, after commissions and repairs, beside a direct offer, and count the weeks as well as the dollars.

On either route the deed is recorded in Harrisburg and the county tax split stays the same.

faqs.q: Who bills real estate tax in Susquehanna Township?
faqs.a: The Dauphin County Treasurer, at 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg. The phone number is 717-780-6550.

faqs.q: What transfer tax comes with a Susquehanna Township sale?
faqs.a: Two percent of the price: 1 percent to the state and half a percent each to the municipality and school district.

faqs.q: Where is a Susquehanna Township deed recorded?
faqs.a: In Dauphin County. The Recorder of Deeds is in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Harrisburg, and the office holds deeds back to 1785.

faqs.q: Which building codes does the township follow?
faqs.a: Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code governs building work, and the township uses the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code for existing buildings, effective July 19, 2022. Residential permit questions go to 717-909-9251.

faqs.q: How much has Susquehanna Township grown?
faqs.a: The population was 24,036 in 2010 and 26,736 in 2020, and it is now estimated at 28,434. That is growth of about 6.2 percent since the 2020 base.
